changelog.change: Added a 2025 evidence-update section (Robba et al., Intensive Care Med 2025): the three ICP-monitoring positions (BTF / Milan / Seattle), a PaO2 target band with a hyperoxaemia caution, no TXA benefit in isolated TBI, CPPopt, the elderly SBP target, and where brain-tissue-oxygen monitoring stands (BOOST-II / OXY-TC / BONANZA-BOOST-III). Adjusted the SpO2/PaO2 target row.
Added whyThisMatters + clinicalTakeaway (standard Reference Library template, DIRECTIONS_FORWARD §1).
Initial entry — BTF physiologic targets, the hyperosmolar-therapy dosing table, and the tiered ICP-management staircase.

summary: Treat ICP > 22 mmHg. Keep CPP 60–70 (CPP = MAP − ICP), MAP ≥ 80, SpO2 ≥ 95%, PaCO2 35–45. Escalate through tiers — head-of-bed and sedation before osmotherapy before paralysis / hyperventilation / barbiturates / decompressive craniectomy. A single episode of hypotension or hypoxia markedly worsens outcome.
whyThisMatters: In severe TBI the brain has almost no reserve, and a single episode of hypotension or hypoxia markedly worsens outcome — so management is as much about relentlessly protecting perfusion and oxygenation as it is about lowering the ICP number.
clinicalTakeaway: Treat ICP > 22. Keep CPP 60–70 (MAP − ICP), MAP ≥ 80, SpO₂ ≥ 95%, PaCO₂ 35–45, and avoid any hypotension or hypoxia. Escalate in tiers — head-up positioning and sedation, then osmotherapy, then paralysis / brief hyperventilation / barbiturates / decompression — not straight to the aggressive options.

rows: 60–70 mmHg (avoid aggressive CPP > 70 with fluids/pressors — ARDS risk)
SpO2 > 94%, PaO2 80–120 mmHg — avoid hypoxia AND hyperoxaemia (PaO2 > 150 increasingly viewed as harmful, not just wasteful)
35–45 mmHg (transient 30–35 only as a bridge in active herniation)
HOB 30°, head midline, no tight collar / ties (jugular outflow)
Avoid hyponatraemia; if using HTS, target 145–155 mEq/L
Prophylactic levetiracetam / phenytoin for 7 days after severe TBI reduces EARLY seizures (no effect on late epilepsy)
Osmotic diuretic — depletes intravascular volume; hold if serum osmolality > 320 or the patient is hypotensive / volume-deplete. Follow the osmolar gap
Central preferred (3% peripheral is acceptable short-term)
Expands volume — better in a hypotensive patient. Check Na⁺ q4–6 h; ceiling ~155–160
Herniation rescue — rapid, brief ↑ Na⁺. Have it drawn up and labelled for the crashing patient

body.text: See the hyperosmolar-therapy module for the mannitol-vs-HTS decision (volume status, renal function, sodium trajectory drive the choice).

items: Tier 0 (all patients): HOB 30°, head midline, normothermia, normocapnia, normoglycaemia, adequate analgesia + light sedation, treat pain/agitation/shivering, keep MAP for CPP 60–70, treat seizures. Get an EVD (also allows CSF drainage) or an ICP monitor for GCS ≤ 8 with an abnormal CT.
Tier 1: increase sedation / analgesia (propofol, fentanyl); CSF drainage via the EVD; a bolus of osmotherapy (mannitol or HTS); ensure the PaCO2 is at the low-normal end (35).

Tier 2: neuromuscular blockade (bolus, then infusion if it works); a trial of higher CPP (up to 70) or a cautious lower-CPP (Lund) approach depending on autoregulation; repeat CT to look for a new surgical lesion.

Tier 3: pentobarbital coma titrated to burst-suppression on continuous EEG (needs vasopressors — myocardial depression); mild hypothermia 35–36 °C (does NOT improve outcome as prophylaxis — POLAR, Eurotherm — reserve as an ICP-control measure); DECOMPRESSIVE CRANIECTOMY (RESCUEicp: lower mortality but more survivors in a vegetative / severely disabled state — a goals-of-care conversation).
Brief hyperventilation to PaCO2 30–35 is a Tier-2/3 temporising measure for impending herniation only — sustained hyperventilation causes ischaemia.

body.text: Herniation now (blown pupil, extensor posturing, Cushing's triad — hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respiration): HOB up, hyperventilate transiently, 23.4% saline 30 mL (or mannitol 1 g/kg), drain CSF if an EVD is in, and call neurosurgery for emergent decompression / evacuation.
2025 evidence update (Robba et al., Intensive Care Med)

items: ICP monitoring is standard of care but has never been shown in an RCT to improve outcome — it detects an expanding mass lesion and informs the wider physiology (CPP, autoregulation, compensatory reserve), it is not a validated treatment target on its own. Three positions on WHEN to monitor: BTF (comatose + abnormal CT, or normal CT plus 2 of age > 40 / hypotension / posturing); the more conservative 2013 Milan consensus (only when a sedation-hold neuro check is genuinely unsafe, or post-craniectomy to gauge effect); and the more liberal Seattle SIBICC Delphi position. No consensus — practice varies.
Blood pressure: SBP ≥ 100 mmHg (age-based) or MAP > 80; SBP ≥ 110 may specifically benefit elderly patients.
CPP: BTF target 60–70; individualised CPPopt (the CPP at which autoregulation is best preserved, from PRx) is of growing interest but the outcome evidence is still catching up.

Fluids: isotonic crystalloid is first-line for resuscitation — routine hypertonic saline has not shown an outcome benefit over isotonic fluid (it remains a tool for acute ICP crises); hypo-osmolar fluids worsen oedema and are contraindicated.

Tranexamic acid: no outcome benefit in ISOLATED TBI despite its reflexive use in trauma (CRASH-3 — the pre-specified benefit was confined to mild–moderate TBI treated within 3 h, and even that is debated). Give it for the coexisting extracranial haemorrhage, not for the head injury itself.

Brain-tissue oxygen (PbtO2) monitoring: BOOST-II cut the burden of brain hypoxia with a non-significant outcome trend; OXY-TC found no overall functional benefit (a signal reappeared in the raised-ICP subgroup). Two phase-III trials (BONANZA, BOOST-III) are running to settle whether ICP + PbtO2 beats ICP alone — a plausible but unproven upgrade for now. Pupillometry, transcranial Doppler, and optic-nerve-sheath diameter have real bedside utility as non-invasive adjuncts.

Despite the thin RCT base for the bundle as a whole, protocolised early control of oxygenation, CO2, BP/CPP, temperature, glucose, and sodium is consistently associated with better survival — the aggregate habit outperforms any single proven component.
